morningLine: Tramiel takes Atari, the IIc travels light, and The Hulk tops the Atari software counter.

lead.headline: Jack Tramiel Takes Atari as Warner Retreats
lead.dek: The Commodore founder acquires Atari's home-computer and console operations, setting up a fierce new round in the personal-computer price war.
body: Warner Communications sold Atari's loss-plagued home-computer and home-video-game operations on Monday, July 2, to a new company headed by Jack Tramiel. Warner kept the coin-operated arcade operation, while the consumer business became the foundation of a new Atari Corporation.

The transaction was valued in contemporary follow-up accounts at roughly $240 million, paid chiefly through notes and warrants rather than a simple cash purchase. It closes Warner's bruising attempt to hold together entertainment, consoles and personal computers after the 1983 video-game collapse produced catastrophic losses.

Tramiel left Commodore only about six months ago. His return at Atari turns two of the home-computer trade's best-known names into direct rivals and puts an operator famous for aggressive pricing in control of Atari's technology, catalog and dealer presence.

The change arrived with immediate pain. By Friday, July 6, UPI reported another 300 Sunnyvale dismissals, and the New York Times also described layoffs ordered by the new owner. Atari's next machines remain unwritten, but its contest with Commodore has already entered a new chapter.

stories.headline: Apple IIc Packs a Full Apple II into 7.5 Pounds
body: Apple's compact IIc brings a 65C02 processor, 128K of RAM, Applesoft BASIC and a built-in 5.25-inch drive into a 7.5-pound case. Rear connections cover display, printer, modem, mouse, joystick and a second disk drive.

The base machine lists for $1,295, before a $199 green-phosphor monitor or $329 external drive. Apple says 90 percent of a library of roughly 10,000 Apple II programs will run, making compatibility the machine's strongest argument against the IBM PCjr.
Portability still has limits. Apple's planned 80-column LCD is scheduled for fall at $600; until then, the little IIc still needs a television or monitor at its destination.

stories.headline: The Hulk Leads Atari's Living Software Shelf
body: A Calisto Atari chart published July 5 puts Adventure International's The Hulk at No. 1, followed by Cosmi's Slinky and Adventure International's The Count.

Airstrike 2, Aztec Challenge, Zaxxon, Encounter, Rally Speedway, Enchanter and Flak fill out the top ten. The mix of arcade action and text adventure shows a market still buying Atari software even as the company above it changes hands.

stories.headline: Byte Watches Computers and Video Converge
body: Byte's July theme issue, 'Computers and Video,' surveys a field in which home machines are increasingly pitched as graphics, animation and video-production tools rather than calculators with keyboards.

Video digitizing, display hardware and graphics software give context to Atari's enduring value: its television orientation, graphics chips and game experience remain useful assets despite Warner's retreat.

curiosity.headline: Apple's 'Portable' Needed a $600 Screen That Did Not Yet Exist
curiosity.summary: The 7.5-pound Apple IIc was easy to carry, but its promised untethered display was still a future accessory.
curiosity.detail: Creative Computing reported that Apple planned an 80-by-24-character low-power LCD for fall at $600. Until then, owners still needed power gear and a television or monitor.

milestone.title: Jack Tramiel Acquires Atari's Consumer Business
milestone.note: The deal redirected a foundational video-game company, created the platform that would launch the Atari ST, and reshaped the Commodore-Atari rivalry.
